summary: Suggests a way for workstations to dynamically access mail from a mailbox server, called a repository. It was a standard for the SUMEX-AIM community and an experimental proposal for the Internet. It was replaced by RFC 1176 and RFC 1203.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of copying all your mail to your computer, you keep it on a server and look at it from wherever you are.

questions: how did interactive mail access begin
how does interactive mail access protocol work
why use imap instead of local mail storage
subtitle: A protocol for workstations to access mail stored on a remote server.

tldr.problem: As workstations became common, it was impractical for each to store and manage mail. Workstations have unreliable service, can fail, and complicate mail addressing across an organization.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP2 lets a workstation access and manage mail stored on a reliable central server. The server handles mail delivery, storage, and searching. The workstation connects, logs in, and requests messages on demand.
tldr.outcome: IMAP2 pioneered remote mailbox access, allowing users to check mail from anywhere. SNMP later superseded it, but IMAP evolved into IMAP4 and remains the dominant protocol for mail access today.

today: RFC 1064 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 1176 and RFC 1203. The core IMAP concept evolved into IMAP4 (RFC 3501), which is still the standard protocol for remote mailbox access on the Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1064 defines the Interactive Mail Access Protocol, Version 2 (IMAP2), a protocol that lets a workstation connect to a remote mail server to access and manage messages. Instead of copying mail to the workstation, a user logs into the server and works with mail stored there.

IMAP2 is a functional superset of POP2 (RFC 937), offering more sophisticated features like server-side searching, message parsing, and mailbox management. The protocol assumes a reliable connection like TCP and uses port 143 by default.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP2 lets you read your mail from a remote computer instead of storing it all locally. You connect to the mail server, log in, and ask to see specific messages.

sections.title: Why Remote Mail Access Matters
sections.content:
Workstations present four problems for local mail storage. First, workstations are often under user control; a user might consume all system resources or accidentally corrupt the mail system. Second, workstation hardware fails, and repairs take time. A centralized server is more reliable and recovers quickly. Third, when many people have different machines, tracking email addresses becomes complicated. Fourth, heterogeneous workstations make it hard to support complex mail protocols consistently.

IMAP2 solves this by keeping the mailbox on a reliable server while letting users access it from any workstation. The server maintains high availability and can be repaired independently of users' work. Users have a single, memorable email address tied to the server, not to their workstation.
sections.plainLanguage: If your mail is on your computer and your computer breaks, you lose everything. If it's on a server, the server is always running and the people who fix it can repair it without stopping your work.

sections.title: How IMAP2 Works
sections.content:
IMAP2 uses a command-response protocol where each command is tagged with a unique identifier. A client connects, the server sends a greeting, and the client logs in with a user name and password. Once authenticated, the client can select a mailbox (starting with INBOX, the user's primary mailbox).

The client fetches message data using structured operations: FETCH retrieves message content, headers, or metadata; SEARCH identifies messages by date, sender, or keywords; STORE modifies message flags (like marking as read or deleted); COPY moves messages to other mailboxes; and EXPUNGE removes deleted messages. The server can also send unsolicited data, notifying the client of new mail or mailbox changes.
sections.plainLanguage: You send numbered commands to the server. You can ask to see message 5, search for messages from someone, mark a message as read, or move a message to a folder. The server sends back the information with the same number so you know which answer matches your question.

sections.title: Messages and Envelopes
sections.content:
IMAP2 defines three categories of data to fetch: message metadata (internal date, size, and flags), the message envelope (parsed header information like sender, recipients, and subject), and the message body (header and text). The envelope is a structured, unambiguous representation computed by the server by parsing the RFC 822 header; clients do not need to understand RFC 822 themselves.

Message flags include system flags like \\SEEN (message has been read), \\RECENT (just arrived), \\ANSWERED (replied to), \\FLAGGED (marked urgent), and \\DELETED (marked for removal). Servers may support additional user-defined flags. This design lets a sophisticated client display a summary, or a simple client can just fetch the entire message and let its own mail reader handle the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: For each message, the server keeps track of who sent it, who it's for, the subject, and whether you've read it. It can also give you just the headers, just the body, or everything. You don't have to know how to parse email headers; the server does it for you.

sections.title: Protocol Design and Tagging
sections.content:
IMAP2 avoids synchronization problems of earlier protocols (like SMTP and FTP) through its tag-based design. Every client command includes a unique tag; the server echoes the tag in the response. This allows the server to send unsolicited data (like notification of new mail) without breaking the client's ability to match responses to requests. The client can even send multiple commands and process responses as they arrive.

The design also enables a two-process client model. One process sends commands and waits for the response with the matching tag. Another process listens to unsolicited messages from the server and updates a local cache of the mailbox state. This mirrors demand-paged virtual memory: the client holds a partial cache and fetches data on demand.
sections.plainLanguage: Every command gets a number. The server sends back that number with the answer, so you know which answer goes with which question. The server can also send messages anytime, and you'll still know what's what.

sections.title: Status and Legacy
sections.content:
RFC 1064 defines IMAP2, which was published in July 1988 and marked as a standard for the SUMEX-AIM community and an experimental proposal for the Internet. It was quickly superseded by RFC 1176 and RFC 1203, which refined the protocol.

Although IMAP2 itself is now Historic, its core ideas shaped IMAP3 and IMAP4 (RFC 3501), which became the dominant protocol for remote mailbox access on the Internet. Every time a user checks email through a mail client like Outlook or Thunderbird using IMAP, they are using a protocol whose foundations were laid by IMAP2.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP2 was replaced by newer versions pretty quickly, but the basic idea of accessing your mail from a server is still how most people check email today.
